cards.title: Independent Deployability — The Defining Promise
cards.teaser: The core value proposition of microservices is not small services — it is that each service can be deployed, scaled, and retired without coordinating with every other team. Lose independent deployability and you have a distributed monolith with all of the complexity and none of the benefits.

runs.text: Independent deployability

is the capability that justifies the operational overhead of microservices. It means: any single service can go from commit to production on its own schedule, without requiring other services to deploy at the same time.
Three conditions must hold for a service to be truly independently deployable:

items.text: Backward-compatible contracts.
A new version must not break existing consumers. Consumers should not need to redeploy just because the producer changed.
Independent data ownership.
Each service owns its own database schema. Shared schemas create coupling that makes migrations a multi-team coordination event.
Isolated build and deploy pipeline.
The service's path to production is its own. It does not wait on other services' builds to pass.

runs.text: When these conditions are absent, teams slip into "release trains" — scheduled windows where all services deploy together. This recreates the coordination overhead of a monolithic release cycle while distributing the accidental complexity across many repositories. The result is the worst of both worlds.

Sam Newman in Building Microservices (2nd ed., 2021) defines independent deployability as the goal microservice decomposition must serve. If two services cannot be deployed independently, the decomposition boundary is wrong or the interface contract is wrong — the services are logically coupled even if they are physically separate.

Independent deployability means any team can ship their service on Friday afternoon without asking every other team for permission. If you need a company-wide release window, you have a distributed monolith — not microservices.

cards.title: Per-Service Pipelines — Each Service Owns Its CI/CD
cards.teaser: A single shared pipeline that builds all services is a monolith hiding in your CI system. Per-service pipelines give each service autonomous control over its build, test, and deploy lifecycle — enabling the deployment cadence each team actually needs.

runs.text: The corollary to independent deployability is that each service must own its own CI/CD pipeline. A shared pipeline that sequences builds across all services forces services to share a deployment clock — even if the code is technically decoupled.
What a well-designed per-service pipeline contains:

items.text: Build and unit test.
Triggered on every commit. Compiles the service, runs fast unit tests, publishes a versioned container image to a registry.
Contract and integration tests.
Runs consumer-driven contract tests (e.g., Pact) to verify the service still satisfies all known consumers. Runs integration tests against a local or ephemeral environment.
Security scanning.
SAST, dependency vulnerability scan, container image scan — scoped to this service's artifact.
Deploy to staging.
Promotes the image to the shared staging environment. Runs smoke tests.
Deploy to production.
Gated by automated health checks. Uses the deployment strategy appropriate for this service (canary, blue/green, rolling).

runs.text: Per-service pipelines do introduce a coordination challenge: a service team must monitor contract test results across consumer-provider pairs. Consumer-driven contract testing frameworks like Pact solve this with a broker that both sides publish to, so neither side needs to coordinate a shared build.

A common mistake is to share a pipeline template but give services a single "deploy all" job at the end. This preserves the monolith's release coordination while pretending to use microservice patterns. Each service must have a production deploy step that runs independently on its own trigger.

Each service should have its own pipeline — its own way to go from code to production — without waiting for any other service's build to finish. Sharing a pipeline is like sharing a car: whoever needs to go somewhere has to wait for everyone else.

cards.title: Blue/Green Deployment — Atomic Cutover
cards.teaser: Blue/green deployment runs two identical environments simultaneously — one live, one staged with the new version — and switches traffic with a single atomic operation. Rollback is equally atomic: switch back. The cost is double the infrastructure for the duration of the transition.

runs.text: Blue/green deployment is named for the two environments:

items.text: Blue
— the current live environment, running the old version.
Green
— the new environment, running the new version, receiving no production traffic yet.

explanation.code:
BLUE/GREEN DEPLOYMENT

Before cutover:
  ┌────────────────────┐    ┌────────────────────┐
  │   BLUE (v1.2)      │    │   GREEN (v1.3)      │
  │   [live traffic]   │    │   [no traffic]      │
  │                    │    │   ← deploy & test   │
  └────────────────────┘    └────────────────────┘
         ▲
  Load Balancer

Cutover (atomic):
  ┌────────────────────┐    ┌────────────────────┐
  │   BLUE (v1.2)      │    │   GREEN (v1.3)      │
  │   [standby]        │    │   [live traffic]    │
  │   ← kept warm      │    │                    │
  └────────────────────┘    └────────────────────┘
                                    ▲
                             Load Balancer

Rollback (if needed):
  Flip load balancer back to BLUE — instant.

runs.text: The mechanism is typically a load balancer or DNS swap — one configuration change moves 100% of traffic from blue to green. Because the swap is atomic, there is no window during which some requests hit v1.2 and others hit v1.3.
Properties of blue/green per service in a microservices system:

items.text: Rollback speed.
A bad deploy rolls back in seconds — just point the load balancer back at blue.
Testing in production.
The green environment can be tested with synthetic traffic or internal users before the cutover.
Database compatibility requirement.
Both versions must be able to operate against the same database state during the transition. This constrains how schema changes can be made (see Expand/Contract card).
Cost.
Running two full environments requires 2x the capacity, even if only briefly. In Kubernetes, blue/green is often approximated by running two Deployments and swapping the Service selector.

runs.text: Blue/green is like painting a new room while the old one is still occupied. You finish the new room completely, move everyone in with one motion, and the old room is immediately available as a fallback.

cards.title: Canary Deployment — Gradual Percentage Rollout
cards.teaser: Canary deployment sends a small percentage of production traffic to the new version while the majority continues hitting the old version. Problems surface on a limited blast radius — if the canary is bad, most users never experienced it.

runs.text: The name comes from the mining practice of using canaries to detect toxic gas: if the canary dies, miners know danger is present before it reaches them. In deployment, the "canary" is the small group of users who receive the new version first.

explanation.code:
CANARY DEPLOYMENT

Phase 1 — Initial release:
  Incoming traffic (100%)
         │
         ├──── 95% ───► [ v1.2 — stable fleet ]
         │
         └────  5% ───► [ v1.3 — canary ]
                              ↑ monitor error rate,
                                latency, business metrics

Phase 2 — Expand (if healthy):
  Incoming traffic (100%)
         │
         ├──── 50% ───► [ v1.2 — stable fleet ]
         │
         └──── 50% ───► [ v1.3 — expanding canary ]

Phase 3 — Full rollout:
  Incoming traffic (100%)
         │
         └── 100% ───► [ v1.3 — now the stable fleet ]

  Abort at any phase: drain canary traffic back to v1.2

runs.text: Traffic routing in a canary is typically controlled by a service mesh (Istio, Linkerd), an API gateway, or a load balancer with weighted routing rules. Kubernetes itself does not natively support percentage-based canary routing — it is simulated by replica count ratios across two Deployments, which is imprecise.
Key properties of canary deployments:

items.text: Progressive delivery.
The percentage expands automatically based on SLO gates: if error rate stays below 0.1% and p99 latency stays under 200ms for 10 minutes, advance to the next percentage increment.
Blast radius control.
A bug at 5% canary affects 5% of users. Fast automated abort minimizes this further.
Both versions run simultaneously.
The new version must be API-compatible with the old: consumers cannot distinguish which version they hit on any given request.

runs.text: Canary deployment is like opening a new restaurant location quietly, sending 5% of customers there, watching if anything goes wrong, and only advertising it broadly after you are confident it works. If the kitchen catches fire, you just reroute everyone back to the original location.

cards.title: Rolling Updates — Incremental Instance Replacement
cards.teaser: A rolling update replaces old instances with new ones one at a time (or in small batches), keeping the service continuously available throughout the process. It is the Kubernetes default — simple to operate, but it comes with a period where both versions coexist.

runs.text: In a rolling update, the deployment controller terminates old pods and starts new ones incrementally. At no point does the total pod count drop below the configured minimum. The process:

items.text: Spin up new pod (v1.3).
Wait for its readiness probe to pass.
Terminate one old pod (v1.2).
Traffic is drained before termination.
Repeat
until all old pods are replaced.

runs.text: Kubernetes controls the pace with two parameters:

items.text: maxSurge
— how many additional pods can exist above the desired count during the update.
maxUnavailable
— how many pods can be unavailable during the update.

runs.text: The critical implication for microservices: during a rolling update, both v1.2 and v1.3 are live simultaneously. Requests from a single user session may hit either version. This means:

items.text: The new version must handle requests that were initiated against the old version.
Database schema changes cannot be additive-only — they must be backward-compatible for the rollout window.
API contracts must be honored by both versions for the duration of the overlap.

runs.text: Rolling updates are the right default for stateless services with backward-compatible changes. For schema-breaking changes or stateful services, blue/green provides a cleaner transition point with a more controllable cutover.

A rolling update replaces one waiter at a time in a restaurant while it stays open. For a few minutes, you might have old-menu waiters and new-menu waiters working the floor at the same time — so both need to know how to handle any order.

cards.title: Shadow Deployment — Dark Launch
cards.teaser: Shadow deployment (also called dark launch) routes a copy of real production traffic to the new version, but the new version's responses are discarded — users see only the old version's response. The new version runs for real, under real load, with zero user impact.

runs.text: Shadow deployment is the most conservative testing strategy before full release. It answers the question: "How does the new version actually behave under real production traffic patterns?" — without exposing users to any risk.

explanation.code:
SHADOW DEPLOYMENT

  Incoming request
         │
         ▼
  [ Load Balancer / Proxy ]
         │
         ├──── response → User ◄─── [ v1.2 — live ]
         │
         └──────────────────────── [ v1.3 — shadow ]
                                        ↑
                         receives copy of request,
                         response is discarded,
                         metrics and logs are captured

runs.text: Use cases for shadow deployments:

items.text: Performance validation.
Verify that the new version handles production traffic volume without latency regression before any users see it.
Correctness verification.
Compare response payloads between v1.2 and v1.3 for the same inputs to catch behavioral divergence.
ML model validation.
A new ML model can process real production inputs and log predictions without serving them. Results are compared offline to verify improvement.

runs.text: Important constraints: shadow traffic must not trigger side effects in the new version. If the new version writes to a database, sends emails, or calls external APIs, shadow mode will cause duplicate side effects. Shadow testing works best for read-heavy workloads or when the new version's side effects can be isolated to a separate data store.

Shadow deployment is like having a student surgeon observe and shadow every procedure without ever holding a scalpel. The student sees real cases, makes real decisions, but all actual cuts are still made by the senior surgeon.

cards.title: Feature Flags — Decoupling Deploy from Release
cards.teaser: A feature flag is a runtime configuration switch that controls whether a feature is active. Deploying code with a feature flag disabled is a non-event — the code is in production but the feature is not released. Release becomes a business decision, not a deployment event.

runs.text: Feature flags — also called feature toggles or feature switches — break the assumed equivalence between "deploy" and "release." Without flags, shipping a feature to users requires deploying code to production. With flags, deployment and release are two independent operations.

items.text: Deploy
— move the compiled artifact to the production environment. A technical event. Reversible with rollback.
Release
— make the feature available to users. A business event. Controlled by a flag flip.

runs.text: Feature flag types by purpose:

items.text: Release flags.
Short-lived. Control rollout of a new feature. Should be removed once the feature is fully released. Accumulation of stale release flags is a maintenance hazard.
Experiment flags.
A/B testing. Route a percentage of users to variant A or B. Governed by the experimentation platform.
Ops flags.
Kill switches for expensive features under load. "If database queue depth exceeds 10,000, disable personalization." Long-lived.
Permission flags.
Control feature access by user tier or account. "Beta users see this feature; general users do not." Long-lived.

runs.text: Feature flags are technical debt by construction. Every flag adds a conditional code path that must be tested in both states. Pete Hodgson's taxonomy (martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html) recommends treating release flags as temporary scaffolding: schedule their removal at creation time.

A feature flag is a light switch in your code. You deploy the wiring to every house in town, but you control which houses actually have the lights turned on. Deploy and release are now separate events under your control.

cards.title: Schema Migration Coordination — The Hardest Part of Microservice Deployment
cards.teaser: Code changes are easy to roll back. Database schema changes are not. Schema migration in a microservices system must be coordinated with the service deployment lifecycle — every schema change must be safe to apply before, during, and after a rolling deployment of the service that owns it.

runs.text: Schema migrations are the point where independent deployability is most threatened. A migration that removes a column breaks the old version of the service still running during a rolling update. A migration that renames a column breaks every consumer that queries that column directly (which, in a properly designed microservices system, should be none — but not every system is properly designed).
The challenge is temporal: during any deployment strategy except an atomic cutover, two versions of the service coexist. The schema must be valid for both.

items.text: Safe schema changes
— adding a nullable column, adding a new table, adding a new index. These do not break the running old version.
Unsafe schema changes
— removing a column, renaming a column, changing a column's type, tightening a constraint. These break the old version.

runs.text: The solution is to never perform an unsafe schema change directly. Instead, use the Expand/Contract pattern to decompose every schema change into a sequence of safe steps (see next card).

Flyway and Liquibase both enforce schema migration versioning. This is necessary but not sufficient: a numbered migration that drops a column is still a breaking change, regardless of whether Flyway ran it. The migration tool enforces order; the expand/contract pattern enforces safety.

Migrating a database schema is like renovating a building while people are still working in it. You cannot knock down a load-bearing wall on a Tuesday afternoon. Every structural change needs to be staged so the building never becomes uninhabitable during the process.

cards.title: Expand/Contract Pattern — Safe Additive Migration
cards.teaser: The expand/contract pattern decomposes any breaking schema change into three safe deployment steps: expand (add the new thing alongside the old), migrate (write to both, backfill data), then contract (remove the old thing after all consumers have moved). At no point is either the old or new version broken.

runs.text: Expand/contract is the standard technique for zero-downtime database migrations. It works by making changes additive first, then removing the old structure only after the new one is fully adopted. The example below renames a column
user_name
to
username
without downtime:
Each phase maps to a deployment:

items.text: Deploy 1 (Expand).
Runs the expand migration. Deploys a new service version that writes to both columns. Old service version continues to work because
user_name
still exists.
Deploy 2 (Migrate).
Backfill script runs. Both columns now contain consistent data. New service version reads from
username
only.
Deploy 3 (Contract).
After old service is fully replaced, drop the old column. Now safe — no running code references
user_name

runs.text: Expand/contract is like adding a new exit to a building before closing the old one. First you build the new door (expand), then you make sure everyone knows how to use it (migrate), then you brick up the old door once no one is using it anymore (contract).

cards.title: Database per Service — Schema Migrations Are Local
cards.teaser: Each microservice owns exactly one database, and no other service may access that database directly. This makes schema migrations a local concern: only one team's deployment pipeline touches one schema. Cross-service schema coupling is a design error.

runs.text: The database-per-service pattern is the data ownership rule that makes independent deployability possible at the schema level. When multiple services share a database, any schema change is a multi-team coordination event: every team that reads from the affected tables must certify that the change does not break their service.
With database per service:

items.text: Schema migrations run in the owning service's pipeline.
No other team's approval is needed.
The migration tool (Flyway, Liquibase) is invoked as a step in the service's deploy job.
Migrations run before the new service version starts receiving traffic.
Data owned by a service is exposed only via the service's API.
Other services query through the API, not through direct SQL joins.

runs.text: Practical isolation strategies when a full separate database engine is too expensive:

items.text: Separate database instance.
Full isolation. Ideal, but has cost and operational overhead.
Separate schema in the same database engine.
A Postgres schema (namespace) per service on the same Postgres instance. Credentials scoped to the owning schema prevent cross-service access.
Separate table prefix convention.
Softer isolation. Enforced by convention and code review rather than access control. Appropriate for startups; not appropriate for production microservices at scale.

runs.text: A shared database is the most common reason microservice decompositions fail to deliver independent deployability. If teams share a database, they share a deployment coupling even if the application code is separate. Fix the data boundary before fixing the service boundary.

Each service gets its own filing cabinet and no one else has the key. If you want data from another service's cabinet, you ask that service — you do not pick the lock. This makes each team the only team that needs to agree to reorganize their own files.

cards.title: Versioned APIs — Supporting Multiple Consumer Versions
cards.teaser: API versioning is the mechanism that lets a service evolve without breaking consumers. By supporting multiple API versions simultaneously, the service provider can deploy v2 while consumer teams migrate from v1 on their own schedule — preserving independent deployability on both sides.

runs.text: In a microservices system, consumers and providers evolve at different rates. A provider cannot require all consumers to deploy simultaneously — that would recreate the release train. API versioning breaks this coupling.
Common versioning schemes:

items.text: URL path versioning.
/api/v1/orders
and
/api/v2/orders
coexist. Simple to implement and cache. The most common approach.
Header versioning.
Accept: application/vnd.stackspeak.v2+json
. Cleaner URLs, but harder to debug and cache.
Query parameter versioning.
/orders?version=2
. Simple but non-RESTful.

runs.text: Version lifecycle management:

items.text: Deprecation notice.
When a new version is released, the old version is marked deprecated with a sunset date communicated via documentation and, ideally, response headers (
Deprecation: date
Sunset: date
Migration window.
Both v1 and v2 are supported in production for a defined period (e.g., 90 days) to give consumer teams time to migrate.
Retirement.
After the sunset date, v1 is removed. Consumer teams that have not migrated will see failures.

runs.text: Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact) is a complementary technique: consumers publish their expectations of the provider API to a broker. Before a provider deploys, its pipeline verifies that the new version satisfies all registered consumer contracts. This catches breaking changes before they reach production.

API versioning is like publishing a book in a new edition while the old edition is still on shelves. Readers using the first edition are not affected when you publish the second. Eventually you stop printing the first edition, but you give everyone enough notice.

cards.title: Rollback Strategies — What "Undo" Actually Means
cards.teaser: Rollback is not a single action — it is a spectrum from "point load balancer at old image" to "run a schema migration in reverse." Each layer of the stack (code, configuration, data) has different rollback characteristics. Designing deployments for rollback is as important as designing them for success.

runs.text: When a deployment fails or causes a production incident, the response options are:

items.text: Redeploy old image.
The fastest option. Works for code-only changes when the old container image is still tagged and available in the registry. Most teams keep the previous N images for exactly this reason.
Feature flag rollback.
For features gated by flags, disable the flag without any deployment. Sub-second. The cleanest rollback when the feature has been deployed with a flag from the start.
Blue/green reverse cutover.
If blue/green was used and the old environment (blue) is still warm, point the load balancer back. Sub-second cutover.
Schema rollback.

The hardest case. If a migration ran, reversing it requires a down-migration. Down-migrations are risky when data has already been written to the new schema. This is why schema migrations should use expand/contract — the expand phase is always safely reversible before the contract phase runs.

runs.text: Rollback readiness checklist:

items.text: The previous container image is tagged and available in the registry.
The deployment pipeline supports a "rollback" trigger that redeploys the previous image.
Rollback has been tested — not just planned. Runbooks are not enough; the action must be practiced.
Schema changes are tracked separately from code changes. Rollback of code does not automatically reverse schema changes.

runs.text: Rolling back code is like pressing Ctrl+Z — it works as long as nothing else has happened since the change. Rolling back a database schema change is like trying to un-bake a cake. Design your migrations so the "un-bake" step is never needed during a normal rollback.

cards.title: Deployment Manifest — Declarative Deployment Spec
cards.teaser: A deployment manifest is the authoritative, version-controlled specification of how a service should be deployed: its image, resource limits, replicas, health checks, environment variables, and network policies. Helm charts and Kubernetes manifests are the dominant forms. The manifest is infrastructure as code for a single service.

runs.text: A deployment manifest declares the desired state of the service in the deployment environment. The deployment controller (Kubernetes, ECS, Nomad) is responsible for making actual state match desired state. The benefits of this declarative model:

items.text: Reproducibility.
Every environment runs the same manifest (with environment-specific values injected via Helm values or Kustomize overlays). No undocumented differences between staging and production.
Auditability.
The manifest is in version control. Every change to resource limits, replica counts, or environment variables is a commit with an author and a message.
Self-healing.
The controller continuously reconciles actual state against the manifest. If a pod crashes, Kubernetes restarts it without human intervention.

runs.text: A minimal Kubernetes deployment manifest for a microservice:

explanation.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
  labels:
    app: order-service
    version: "1.3.2"
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-service
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0        # zero-downtime: never terminate before new pod is ready
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-service
        version: "1.3.2"
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-service
          image: registry.example.com/order-service:1.3.2
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "256Mi"
              cpu: "250m"
            limits:
              memory: "512Mi"
              cpu: "500m"
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health/ready
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health/live
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
            periodSeconds: 10

runs.text: In a Helm chart, the image tag and replica count become parameterized values injected at deploy time by the pipeline:

explanation.code:
helm upgrade order-service ./charts/order-service \
  --set image.tag=${GIT_SHA} \
  --set replicaCount=3 \
  --namespace production

runs.text: A deployment manifest is the blueprint for how a service runs — not a script of steps to execute, but a description of the desired end state. The deployment system reads the blueprint and figures out how to get there. Change the blueprint, and the system automatically adjusts.

cards.title: The Deploy-on-Friday Anti-Pattern — Culture vs. Capability
cards.teaser: "We don't deploy on Fridays" is not a safety practice — it is an admission that deployments are dangerous and rollbacks are unreliable. Charity Majors argues that if you cannot safely deploy on Friday afternoon, the problem is your deployment process, not the calendar.

runs.text: The "no deploy on Friday" rule is one of the most widely accepted conventions in software engineering. The reasoning: if something breaks on Friday afternoon, the on-call engineer faces a production incident over the weekend with reduced team capacity to help.
Charity Majors (CTO of Honeycomb, co-author of
Observability Engineering

) has written and spoken extensively on why this convention is a symptom, not a solution. Her position: the rule exists because deployments are batched (too many changes at once), observability is poor (you cannot tell quickly if something is wrong), and rollback is slow or manual. If you fix those three things, the day of the week becomes irrelevant.

items.text: Batched deployments are riskier.

If you deploy once a week on Thursday, each deployment contains five days of accumulated changes. The blast radius is five times larger than daily deployments. Teams that deploy multiple times per day have smaller, safer deploys — the day of the week does not matter.
Poor observability makes any deployment risky.
If you cannot tell within 60 seconds whether a deploy is healthy, you are flying blind regardless of the day. Instruments — not calendars — provide safety.
Slow rollback makes every outage worse.
If rollback takes 30 minutes and requires three humans on a call, Friday is dangerous. If rollback takes 30 seconds and is fully automated, Friday is fine.

runs.text: Majors' framing: "Not deploying on Fridays is a risk management strategy for teams with poor deployment hygiene. Fix the hygiene. DORA's elite performers deploy multiple times per day — they do not have deploy-free days." The goal is to make every deploy so small and so observable that no day of the week is meaningfully riskier than any other.

This does not mean Friday deploys are mandatory. It means: if your process is good enough, Friday is a valid choice. The rule should be "deploy when you have high confidence" — not "never deploy on a specific calendar day."

"No deploys on Friday" is like saying "don't drive on rainy days" — it addresses the symptom (driving is dangerous in bad conditions) instead of the cause (your car's brakes are bad). Fix the brakes and you can drive in the rain.

cards.title: Deployment Topology — Wiring It All Together
cards.teaser: The full deployment topology of a microservices system connects per-service pipelines, deployment manifests, environment promotion, observability, and rollback into a coherent operational model. Each service is an independent unit; the system as a whole still needs operational discipline to remain governable.

runs.text: A mature microservices deployment topology has several distinct layers, each governed by the patterns in this chapter:

explanation.code:
MICROSERVICES DEPLOYMENT TOPOLOGY

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Service Repository (e.g., order-service)                    │
  │                                                              │
  │  commit → per-service pipeline:                             │
  │    [build] → [unit test] → [contract test]                  │
  │      → [security scan] → [push image]                       │
  │        → [deploy staging] → [smoke test]                    │
  │          → [deploy prod: canary 5%]                         │
  │            → [SLO gate: 10 min] → [expand to 100%]          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
           │                          │
           │ (contract test results)  │ (image tag)
           ▼                          ▼
  ┌──────────────┐          ┌─────────────────────┐
  │  Pact Broker │          │  Container Registry  │
  └──────────────┘          └─────────────────────┘
                                      │
                            ┌─────────┴──────────┐
                            │                    │
                     ┌──────▼──────┐    ┌────────▼────────┐
                     │  Staging    │    │   Production     │
                     │  Namespace  │    │   Namespace      │
                     │  (K8s)      │    │   (K8s)          │
                     └─────────────┘    └─────────────────┘

runs.text: Governance concerns that cut across all services:

items.text: Deployment frequency tracking.
DORA metrics are per-service and aggregated. Teams should know their individual deployment frequency and MTTR.
Manifest review policy.
Changes to deployment manifests (resource limits, replica counts, security contexts) may require platform team review in regulated environments.
Shared observability stack.
Each service's canary and rollout health is monitored by a shared platform: a spike in error rate in any service's canary triggers an alert.
Dependency-aware promotion.
When a provider service changes its API, the contract test broker notifies all consumer pipelines. Consumers can block their own deploy until the new contract is validated.

runs.text: Independent deployability does not mean governance-free deployment. It means the governance is automated and per-service, not manual and cross-service. The platform enforces standards; teams retain autonomy within those standards.

Each service deploys independently, but all services deploy into the same production environment. The deployment topology is what keeps the whole system coherent — each service owns its pipeline but shares the runway.
